tagline: Mature trees and harbor views along Bristol’s streets and parade route.
intro: A canopy of mature trees lines nearly the entire Bristol scenic roadway, linking the Warren town line with the Mount Hope Bridge. Rhode Island designated five miles of Route 114, including Hope Street and Ferry Road, and High Street in August 2000. RIDOT highlights the trees, historic homes and seventeenth-century street grid, with side-street views of Bristol Harbor and Poppasquash Point.

The town’s proprietors laid out Bristol’s original center in 1680, with the Town Common part of that plan. At the southern end of the corridor, a ferry once connected Bristol and Portsmouth. Construction of the Mount Hope Bridge began in 1927; structural problems forced parts to be dismantled and reassembled before its opening in October 1929.

Drive south from the Warren line along Hope Street, passing the entrance to Colt State Park before Bristol’s historic center. The waterfront district extends south to Walker Cove. On Ferry Road, Blithewold’s mansion and arboretum occupy a harbor-side estate; farther south, the two-lane Mount Hope Bridge carries Route 114 toward Portsmouth.
notice: Side streets in the historic district frame views of Bristol Harbor and Poppasquash Point.

moments.title: Colt State Park
moments.text: Conrad and Pomeroy, two bronze bulls, mark Colt State Park’s main entrance on Hope Street. Their gate carries the inscription “Colt Farm. Private Property, Public Welcome.” Beginning in 1905, industrialist Samuel P. Colt combined three farms and built a summer house and a stone barn for Jersey cattle. His will required the farm to remain open to the public. Rhode Island took the property by eminent domain in 1965 and dedicated the park in 1968. The summer house was demolished in the 1960s, but the stone cow barn survives.

moments.title: Hope Street
moments.text: Hope Street carries Route 114 through a town whose Independence Day celebration began in 1785. The Reverend Henry Wight, a Revolutionary War veteran at the First Congregational Church, established the Patriotic Exercises that year. Bristol has celebrated the Fourth every year since, although the parade itself has been canceled several times. The Bristol Fourth of July Committee continues to organize the festivities. Beyond the celebration, the street belongs to a seventeenth-century planned grid, with cross streets opening toward the harbor and Poppasquash Point.

moments.title: Ferry Road
moments.text: Blithewold at 101 Ferry Road gives this part of the drive a documented connection to Bristol’s summer estates. Augustus and Bessie Van Wickle established the mansion and grounds in the 1890s as a summer retreat. Their 1895 Queen Anne house burned and was replaced in 1906 by Blithewold II, designed in English Country Manor style by Walter Kilham. The grounds chiefly reflect John DeWolf’s designs from 1896 to 1913. The arboretum and gardens contain more than 300 species of woody plants, including native and exotic species.
